classification.difficultyReason: Explain when signed linear cases require a nonnegative-right-side check, distinguish a variable right side from a positive constant, and justify why equality of two absolute values introduces no sign-invalid candidates.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Explain why when solving, we need to test the solutions of the equation $|2x-1|=x$, but not the solutions of the equation $|2x-1|=1$.

answer.short: For $|2x-1|=x$, candidates must satisfy $x\geq0$. For $|2x-1|=1$, the right side is already nonnegative, so both linear cases are valid.
answer.worked:
For $|2x-1|=x$, the left side is nonnegative, so the right side must satisfy $x\geq0$. Candidates obtained from $2x-1=\pm x$ must meet this condition. Here they are $1$ and $\frac13$, and both do.

For $|2x-1|=1$, the right side is the positive constant $1$. The cases $2x-1=1$ and $2x-1=-1$ are equivalent to the original equation, so they introduce no sign-invalid candidates.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Do we need to test the solutions of $|2x-1|=|x|$? Justify your answer.

answer.short: No additional sign check is needed: both sides are nonnegative, and $|2x-1|=|x|$ is equivalent to $2x-1=x$ or $2x-1=-x$.
answer.worked: For real numbers $A$ and $B$, $|A|=|B|$ exactly when $A=B$ or $A=-B$. Thus the two linear cases are equivalent to the original equation and do not introduce sign-invalid candidates. Both absolute-value sides are nonnegative.
